topic: How to prioritise when everything feels urgent: sort the work by impact and effort, do the high-impact small jobs first, plan the big ones, and say no or later to the rest
scope_note: Prioritising a queue of competing work tasks by impact and effort, plus the urgent versus important distinction, saying no or later, and re-sorting. Not a full time-management course; no productivity statistics.

facts.statement: An impact and effort matrix sorts each task by two questions: how much difference finishing it makes, and how much work it takes.
facts.caveat: This is a widely used planning practice with no single agreed originator; say 'a common way to sort work', not 'a proven method'.
facts.reference_hint: Common practice in project and product prioritisation guides; no single source.

facts.statement: Crossing high or low impact with high or low effort gives four zones: high impact and low effort, high impact and high effort, low impact and low effort, low impact and high effort.
facts.caveat: Zone names vary between sources; the lesson should pick one set and use it consistently.
facts.reference_hint: Common practice; naming varies by author.

facts.statement: The high impact, low effort zone is commonly called quick wins, and the usual advice is to do these first.
facts.caveat: Professional practice guidance, not an experimental result. A quick win still needs a quick check that it is truly high impact.

facts.statement: The high impact, high effort zone is commonly called major projects, and the usual advice is to plan and schedule them deliberately rather than start them in scraps.
facts.caveat: Practice guidance, not an experimental result.

facts.statement: The low impact, low effort zone is commonly called fill-ins, and the usual advice is to batch them or do them in spare moments, or let them wait.
The low impact, high effort zone is commonly called thankless tasks or time sinks, and the usual advice is to decline, drop or park them.
facts.caveat: Practice guidance. Something with low impact for you may matter to someone else, so check before dropping it, and say no openly rather than let it quietly lapse.

facts.statement: Urgency and importance are two separate questions: urgency is about how soon something is wanted, importance is about how much it matters to your goals.
facts.reference_hint: The urgent and important distinction is the basis of the Eisenhower matrix, popularised in Covey, The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989).

facts.statement: Experiments on the mere urgency effect found that people often chose tasks with a nearer deadline over tasks with a bigger payoff, even when the urgent tasks had no advantage other than the deadline.
facts.caveat: Single research line from consumer and decision research, mostly in controlled studies; say 'research suggests we lean toward the nearer deadline', not that it always happens.
facts.reference_hint: Zhu, Yang and Hsee, 'The Mere Urgency Effect', Journal of Consumer Research (2018).

facts.statement: A line often attributed to Eisenhower about urgent and important problems comes from a 1954 speech in which he was quoting someone else, so it should not be presented as his own saying.
facts.caveat: Based on quotation-research accounts of his 1954 Evanston address, which attribute the line to a former college president he quoted. Safest for the script: do not quote it at all; if the matrix is named for Eisenhower, say only that it is named after him.
facts.reference_hint: Eisenhower address to the World Council of Churches assembly, Evanston, 1954; quotation-research accounts such as Quote Investigator.

facts.statement: Effort estimates are often too optimistic, so a task placed as small should be sized with some margin.
facts.caveat: Rests on the planning fallacy, a well-documented tendency to underestimate time and effort; it does not tell how large the error is in any one case.
facts.reference_hint: Planning fallacy: Kahneman and Tversky, work on intuitive prediction.

facts.statement: When saying no or later, tie the answer to your current priorities, so it reads as a reasoned choice rather than a refusal.
facts.caveat: Professional advice from workplace guidance, not a tested script; tone and relationship still matter.
facts.reference_hint: Common workplace-communication guidance; no single source.

facts.statement: When saying later, offer a specific alternative such as a date, a smaller version, or a trade-off, instead of an open-ended maybe.
facts.caveat: Professional advice, not an experimental result.
facts.reference_hint: Common workplace-communication guidance; no single source.

facts.statement: When a request comes from a manager or someone senior, you can ask which existing task should give way, which makes the trade-off visible to them.
facts.caveat: Professional advice; works where the requester has authority to reprioritise, so it fits a manager better than a peer.
facts.reference_hint: Common workplace-communication guidance; no single source.

facts.statement: New requests change the picture, so place each new task on the same matrix when it arrives and re-sort the list, rather than working in arrival order.
facts.caveat: Practice guidance: priorities move, so a brief regular review keeps the sort current. There is no evidence-based ideal review interval.
facts.reference_hint: Common practice in task and project management guidance.

facts.statement: Switching between tasks has a cost in time and accuracy, which is one reason large pieces of work usually go better in protected blocks than in fragments.
facts.caveat: Task-switching costs are well documented in lab studies; how large they are in real office work varies, and the evidence for time blocking itself as a method is mostly practitioner experience. Say 'tends to', give no size.
facts.reference_hint: Task-switching research reviewed in Monsell, 'Task switching', Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2003).

not_claimed: The famous urgent-versus-important line as Eisenhower's own words, or the claim that urgent things are never important
That important work is never urgent, or that urgent work should always be ignored
Any percentage of time or work said to be wasted or low-value, without a source
The Pareto 80/20 rule presented as a law of work
That multitasking makes people more productive
That the impact and effort matrix is scientifically proven to improve output
That people have fixed learning styles
Any invented quote or named expert for the saying-no scripts

terms.meaning: How much difference finishing the task makes to your goals or to others who rely on it.
How much time and work the task takes you.
A task with high impact and low effort.
A task with high impact and high effort.
A task with low impact and low effort.
A task with low impact and high effort, also called a time sink.
